_note: Every date in this file is as published in the cited paper, in years before 1950 (radiocarbon convention where applicable) or as a geological age. Dates are rounded to the precision the source supports. Where the literature disagrees, the disagreement is carried in `contested` rather than resolved here.

species.name: Ardipithecus ramidus
species.note: The earliest well-known hominin skeleton — woodland, not open plain.
species.blurb: The 4.4-million-year-old partial skeleton from Aramis, Ethiopia, shows a creature that climbed in trees and walked upright on the ground. It matters here as the starting line: it says the human line did not begin on a savanna, and it puts the split from the chimpanzee line several million years earlier.

species.name: Australopithecus anamensis
species.note: The oldest known upright walker, from Kanapoi and Allia Bay, Kenya.
species.blurb: Known mainly from jaws and leg bones, it has the oldest securely dated evidence of habitual bipedalism in the hominin line. A 3.8-million-year-old cranium from Woranso-Mille, Ethiopia, sits exactly where anamensis should meet afarensis, which is why the two are usually treated as one evolving line rather than two separated species.

species.name: Australopithecus afarensis
species.note: The best-known early hominin, and the Laetoli footprints.
species.blurb: Lucy, from Hadar, is the reference skeleton for this species, and the 3.66-million-year-old footprint trails at Laetoli in Tanzania are hard evidence of a modern-style upright gait. The shoulders and fingers are still built for climbing, so it is usually read as an animal that did both.

species.name: Australopithecus africanus
species.note: The Taung child's species — the first hominin fossil found in Africa.
species.blurb: Found across the South African caves at Taung, Sterkfontein and Makapansgat. Its hand bones are more human-like than afarensis, which some read as the beginning of tool use — but no stone tools have been found with it.

species.name: Australopithecus sediba
species.note: A mosaic: australopith feet, Homo-like hips and teeth, one short window.
species.blurb: Two partial skeletons from Malapa, South Africa, dated to about 1.98 million years ago. Its brain is small but its teeth and pelvis look like early Homo, which is why it has been proposed as an ancestor of our genus — a claim the field has not settled.

species.name: Paranthropus robustus
species.note: A side branch with enormous teeth and a sagittal crest.
species.blurb: A southern African contemporary of early Homo, built around heavy chewing — large molars, thick enamel, powerful jaw muscles anchored on a bony crest. Its hand bones show it still made and used tools. It is a cousin, not an ancestor.

species.name: Paranthropus boisei
species.note: The eastern twin of robustus, even more extreme in the jaws.
species.blurb: From Olduvai, Lake Turkana and Konso, it coexisted with early Homo for over a million years in the same basins. It lived alongside the first stone-tool makers and was not one of them — the clearest case in this record of two hominins sharing ground without either replacing the other.

species.name: Early Homo — species not identified
species.note: Stone tools older than any fossil that can be named to a species.
species.blurb: The oldest stone tools are older than the oldest fossils that can be assigned to a species with any confidence. Gona in Ethiopia at 2.6 million years, Shangchen on the Chinese Loess Plateau at 2.1, Masol in the Siwaliks at 2.2 — these are the work of hominins nobody can name. They are drawn here as one category on purpose: giving them a species name would be a guess wearing a label.

species.name: Homo habilis
species.note: The first species in our genus: bigger brain, smaller face, oldest tools.
species.blurb: Named in 1964 for fossils from Olduvai Gorge found with the Oldowan stone tools. Its status as a species has been argued about ever since — the material spans a size and shape range that some read as more than one species. It is the first hominin that is comfortably called Homo.

species.name: Homo ergaster
species.note: The Turkana Boy: a tall, long-legged African body plan.
species.blurb: The nearly complete 1.6-million-year-old skeleton from Nariokotome in Kenya is the first hominin with a modern torso, long legs and a narrow pelvis — a body built for walking long distances in the open. Its body proportions differ enough from Asian Homo erectus that the African form is usually given this separate name.

species.name: Homo erectus
species.note: The first hominin out of Africa — and the longest-lived species in our genus.
species.blurb: It left Africa about 1.8 million years ago and reached Georgia, Java and northern China within a few tens of thousands of years, then persisted in island Southeast Asia until roughly 108,000 years ago — after early Homo sapiens had already appeared in Africa. Over that span it is a category more than a single population, and the Asian and African ends of it are probably several species wearing one name.

species.name: Homo antecessor
species.note: The oldest securely dated European human — with cut marks on bones.
species.blurb: From the Gran Dolina level of the Atapuerca caves in northern Spain. Its face looks unexpectedly modern, and a 2020 proteome study placed it close to the last common ancestor of Neanderthals, Denisovans and us — but the protein analysis and the shape of the teeth disagree, and that is unresolved.

species.name: Homo heidelbergensis
species.note: The wide-ranging Middle Pleistocene form of Europe and Africa.
species.blurb: The Sima de los Huesos pit at Atapuerca holds at least 28 individuals dated to about 430,000 years ago, with mitochondrial DNA that already sits on the Neanderthal line. Its DNA shows the Neanderthal–Denisovan split had happened by then — so this fossil is best read as the population Neanderthals came out of, not as a separate ancestor standing beside them.

species.name: Homo rhodesiensis
species.note: The African Middle Pleistocene form, from Bodo and Kabwe.
species.blurb: Large-brained, large-faced archaic humans from Ethiopia, Zambia and Tanzania. Some researchers treat this as the same species as heidelbergensis and others as a separate African one that leads toward us. It is the ancestor question in this period, and the honest answer is that it is not settled.

species.name: Homo naledi
species.note: A small-brained Homo that lived deep in a South African cave system.
species.blurb: Fifteen individuals from the Rising Star cave complex, deliberately carried into a chamber that is very hard to reach, and dated far more recently than their anatomy implies. The hand is built for climbing and for gripping, and the brain is roughly a third of ours. Its date and its behaviour both sit awkwardly inside the standard story, which is why it is contested.

species.name: Homo longi
species.note: A huge East Asian cranium, with affinities argued to be closer to us than to Neanderthals.
species.blurb: The Harbin cranium, from northeastern China. Its one published tree puts it as the sister group to Homo sapiens, with Neanderthals and Denisovans on the other branch. Everybody agrees on the shape; the position is a single analysis, and treating it as a species at all depends on how much variation you allow inside the Asian Middle Pleistocene.

species.name: Nesher Ramla Homo
species.note: A Levantine archaic population that overlapped and probably interbred with early modern humans.
species.blurb: A jaw and skull fragments from a sinkhole near Ramla, Israel, with a mosaic of Neanderthal and archaic features and stone tools matching those of later, local Homo sapiens. The authors argue it represents a Levantine population ancestral to Neanderthals. Its importance here is the date: two different hominins in the same region at the same time.

species.name: Homo neanderthalensis
species.note: Europe and western Asia for 350,000 years, then gone — and still in most of us.
species.blurb: They ranged from Iberia to the Altai, hunted large game, made pigment and adhesive, buried some of their dead, and lived in small groups across a huge range. Their whole population was probably never more than a few tens of thousands, which is why the end can be read either way: they died out, and their genes did not. Every person outside sub-Saharan Africa carries roughly 1.5 to 2 percent Neanderthal ancestry today.

species.name: Homo denisova
species.note: Known almost entirely from DNA — a handful of bones and teeth across Asia.
species.blurb: Named from a single finger bone in Denisova Cave, Siberia, in 2010. They range from the Altai to the Tibetan plateau, and their ancestry survives in living people across island Southeast Asia and Oceania — up to about 5 percent in Papuans, and versions of their genes shape modern Himalayan and Papuan physiology. The end date here is inferred from genetics, not from a dated fossil: no Denisovan fossil younger than about 50,000 years ago is known.

species.name: Homo floresiensis
species.note: A metre-tall island hominin, on Flores from about 700,000 to 60,000 years ago.
species.blurb: From Liang Bua on Flores, Indonesia. A metre tall, about 25 kilograms, with a brain the size of a chimpanzee's, and it made stone tools. Its ancestors reached Flores at least 700,000 years ago, which means a hominin crossed a deep-water strait long before Homo sapiens did. The 2016 re-dating moved its end from 18,000 to about 60,000 years ago — so it was gone before modern people are known to have arrived.

species.name: Homo luzonensis
species.note: A second island hominin, on Luzon, known from hand and foot bones.
species.blurb: From Callao Cave in the northern Philippines: teeth, finger bones and a foot bone from at least three individuals. The hands and feet are a mixture of very old and surprisingly modern traits, which nobody can yet place on a tree. It is known from fewer than a dozen small bones.

species.name: Archaic West African ghost lineage
species.note: A population nobody has ever found a bone from, inferred entirely from living genomes.
species.blurb: Living West Africans carry a few percent of ancestry that is neither modern human nor Neanderthal nor Denisovan. It most likely comes from a population that separated from our line very early and stayed in Africa, meeting modern humans perhaps 20,000 to 50,000 years ago. There is no fossil. There is no name. There is only the signal in the DNA — and that is written on the map as a ghost, marked as one.

species.name: Homo sapiens
species.note: Africa first, then everywhere — the only hominin left.
species.blurb: The oldest fossils that most researchers accept as our species are the 315,000-year-old Jebel Irhoud material from Morocco, and Omo I from Ethiopia is dated to at least 233,000 years. The origin is not a single African valley: it is a set of populations across the continent, changing together. That population left Africa more than once — a failed early dispersal around 180,000 years ago, and the one that worked, from about 70,000 years ago onward.
